question: What is the main job of a medical-surgical nurse?

options.A: Managing administrative budgets for hospital wards and clinics
options.B: Caring for adult patients with various medical illnesses and surgical needs
options.C: Delivering emergency psychiatric interventions in crisis centers
options.D: Providing specialized surgical operations inside the operating theater

explanation: You'll see med-surg nursing everywhere in the hospital! It's all about looking after adults dealing with medical conditions or bouncing back from surgery. You've got this!

question: Why is the med-surg nurse often called the 'heartbeat' of the healthcare team?

options.A: They make all final medical diagnoses and prescribe necessary drug treatments independently
options.B: They perform all surgical operations when the primary surgeon is unavailable
options.C: They coordinate care plans with multiple healthcare professionals and monitor the patient continuously
options.D: They handle all financial billing and hospital admission tasks for every patient department

explanation: Because you're at the bedside the most, you notice the little changes first and help connect the doctors, pharmacists, and therapists. You are truly the team's anchor!

question: What happens first during the assessment phase of the nursing process?

options.A: Evaluating whether the patient has achieved their health goals
options.B: Writing the final medical diagnosis for the patient's chart
options.C: Collecting subjective and objective data about the patient's health status
options.D: Administering prescribed medications and performing wound care procedures

explanation: Assessment is always step one! It's like being a detective—gathering clues by talking to the patient, doing a physical check, and looking at lab results.

question: A nurse checks a patient's blood pressure 30 minutes after giving a blood pressure drug. Which nursing step is this?

options.A: Diagnosis
options.B: Assessment
options.C: Planning
options.D: Evaluation

explanation: Spot-checking to see if your nursing action actually worked is what evaluation is all about. Did the medicine do its job? Let's check!

question: What is the normal blood pH range for a healthy human body?
explanation: Think of 7.35 to 7.45 as the body's sweet spot. Keeping blood slightly alkaline here keeps all our cells and enzymes happy and working smoothly.

question: A patient is suffering from severe diarrhea and vomiting. What condition are they most at risk for?

options.A: Fluid volume deficit
options.B: Metabolic alkalosis
options.C: Respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Fluid volume excess

explanation: When fluids leave the body too fast from both ends, fluid volume drops quickly. That's why rehydration is usually the very first order of business!

question: Which of these is NOT one of the classic local signs of acute inflammation?

options.A: Pain
options.B: Swelling
options.C: Numbness
options.D: Redness

explanation: Remember the classic signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function. Numbness points more toward a nerve issue than simple inflammation!

question: Why do deep, open wounds heal through 'secondary intention' instead of closing right away?

options.A: Surgical stitches dissolve too quickly in infected tissue environments
options.B: Primary intention only applies to burns and skin rashes
options.C: Secondary intention prevents any risk of bacterial contamination
options.D: There is too much tissue loss to pull the wound edges together directly

explanation: When there's a big gap with missing tissue, you can't just stitch it shut. The body has to patiently build new granulation tissue from the bottom up!

question: What is our best and most reliable guide when assessing a patient's pain?

options.A: The patient's own verbal report of the pain
options.B: The underlying surgical diagnosis on the chart
options.C: The family member's description of discomfort
options.D: The nurse's objective observation of vital signs

explanation: Pain is whatever the patient says it is! Because we can't feel it for them, their personal word is always our gold standard.

question: Why do nurses often mix pain meds with comfort measures like positioning and gentle massage?

options.A: Hospital policies strictly forbid using only drugs for post-operative patients
options.B: Non-pharmacological methods can completely replace the need for prescription painkillers
options.C: Medications work much slower if physical comfort measures are skipped
options.D: It targets pain through multiple pathways and reduces reliance on heavy medication doses

explanation: Combining approaches attacks pain from different angles. It helps patients feel better faster while keeping drug side effects as low as possible.

question: What is the top priority for a nurse caring for a patient right after surgery in the recovery room?

options.A: Obtaining the signed surgical consent form from the family
options.B: Assisting the surgeon with closing skin incisions in theater
options.C: Monitoring airway patency, breathing, and vital signs
options.D: Discussing long-term dietary changes for home care

explanation: Airway and breathing always come first! In recovery (PACU), keeping those airways clear and vitals stable is your number one life-saving duty.

question: What is the nurse's specific job when handling a surgical consent form?

options.A: Explaining all potential surgical risks and complications in detail to the patient
options.B: Witnessing the patient's signature after confirming they understand the procedure from the surgeon
options.C: Signing the consent form on behalf of an unconscious patient without family
options.D: Deciding whether the patient is mentally fit to undergo general anesthesia

explanation: The doctor explains the surgery, but you act as the trusted witness to make sure the patient understands and is signing willingly. Teamwork!

question: What is the core problem happening inside the body during all types of shock?

options.A: Inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular oxygenation
options.B: Rapid overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: Sudden elevation in systemic arterial blood pressure
options.D: Excessive accumulation of bicarbonate in the blood

explanation: Shock means the body's tissues aren't getting enough blood flow and oxygen to keep the cells happy. It's an emergency requiring quick action!

question: Which of these is usually one of the very first warning signs that a patient is slipping into shock?

options.A: Restlessness and increased heart rate
options.B: Elevated blood pressure and flushed face
options.C: Slow, bounding pulse and warm skin
options.D: High urine output and deep sleep

explanation: When blood flow dips, the body panics a bit and pumps harder (tachycardia) while the brain gets restless from lack of oxygen. Always trust your instincts when a patient suddenly seems 'off'!

question: What is the main heart and soul of palliative care nursing?

options.A: Improving quality of life and relieving discomfort for serious illnesses
options.B: Shortening the natural dying process to reduce hospital costs
options.C: Preventing family members from visiting patients in final stages
options.D: Finding a permanent cure for terminal infectious diseases

explanation: Palliative care isn't about curing a disease; it's about wrapping the patient and family in comfort, dignity, and gentle symptom relief.

question: How does end-of-life nursing care differ from standard acute hospital care?

options.A: Family members take over all physical nursing duties inside the hospital ward
options.B: Treatment focuses exclusively on aggressive life-support interventions
options.C: Nurses stop monitoring vital signs and administering any form of medication
options.D: Care priorities shift from curing disease to ensuring comfort, dignity, and symptom relief

explanation: When medical cures are no longer possible, our focus shifts beautifully toward peace, pain control, and supporting loved ones through a very tender time.

question: What is the main focus of holistic nursing care?

options.A: Administering prescribed medications on a strict schedule
options.B: Managing hospital equipment and monitoring vital signs
options.C: Treating the whole person including mind, body, and spirit
options.D: Focusing strictly on curing the diagnosed physical disease

explanation: Holistic nursing looks beyond just the physical symptoms to care for every aspect of the human person. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T2#GNS123_U1_T2_h1)

question: How does holistic care differ from traditional medical care that only looks at the disease?

options.A: It focuses only on spiritual counseling during illness
options.B: It integrates physical treatments with emotional and social support
options.C: It completely replaces modern medicine with herbal remedies
options.D: It ignores laboratory results in favor of patient feelings

explanation: Great job! Holistic care doesn't throw out medicine; it simply combines standard medical treatments with a broad view of everything our patients need.

question: Which dimension of holistic care involves a person's sense of meaning, purpose, and faith?

options.A: Spiritual dimension
options.B: Physical dimension
options.C: Social dimension
options.D: Mental dimension

explanation: The spiritual dimension connects a patient to their core values, life purpose, and faith traditions. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T2#GNS123_U1_T2_h2)

question: A patient with severe malaria is worried about losing income and how their family will eat while they are in the hospital. Which dimension of care is primarily affected here?

options.A: Mental dimension
options.B: Physical dimension
options.C: Social dimension
options.D: Spiritual dimension

explanation: Spot on! Family roles, financial worries, and community support fall squarely under the social dimension of human life.

question: Which of these is a great example of an open-ended question you can ask a patient?

options.A: Asking 'How are you coping with your illness today?'
options.B: Nodding silently without asking any questions at all
options.C: Asking 'Did you take your morning blood pressure pill?'
options.D: Telling the patient 'You need to stop worrying so much.'

explanation: Well done! Open-ended questions can't be answered with a simple 'yes' or 'no', which encourages your patient to open up and share more.

question: Why is building a trusting nurse-patient relationship so important for holistic care?

options.A: It allows the nurse to give orders that the patient must follow without question
options.B: It ensures the patient will never complain about hospital food or bills
options.C: It helps patients feel safe enough to share deep fears and personal concerns
options.D: It replaces the need for doctors to visit the patient on the ward

explanation: You got it! Trust creates a safe space where patients feel comfortable revealing the emotional and social burdens that impact their healing.

question: Which of these is a key part of doing a full, holistic nursing assessment?

options.A: Exploring the patient's home support systems and cultural beliefs
options.B: Avoiding questions about mental health to prevent upsetting them
options.C: Rushing the patient to finish answering interview questions quickly
options.D: Focusing exclusively on laboratory values and bedside monitors

explanation: Awesome! Holistic assessments intentionally gather data on social, cultural, and emotional factors right alongside physical signs.

question: Why must a nurse pay attention to non-verbal cues like facial expressions during an assessment?

options.A: Patients may hide their true emotional distress behind polite words
options.B: Non-verbal cues are the only way to measure blood pressure accurately
options.C: Patients expect nurses to read their minds without asking questions
options.D: Hospital regulations require charting body language every hour

explanation: Exactly! People often say they are fine while their body language quietly reveals anxiety, pain, or fear.

question: What is an important safety action when a patient wants to use herbal supplements in the hospital?

options.A: Encourage the patient to double their dosage for faster healing
options.B: Confiscate all herbal products immediately because they are dangerous
options.C: Ignore what the patient takes as long as they swallow their pills
options.D: Screen the supplements for potential interactions with prescribed medications

explanation: Spot on! Herbal products can react strongly with conventional drugs, so as nurses, we always check for safety interactions first.

question: What is the primary role of the nurse when patients want to use complementary or alternative therapies?

options.A: Forbidding patients from using any therapy not written in the doctor's orders
options.B: Personally performing massage and aromatherapy for every single patient
options.C: Ensuring safe use, providing education, and supporting patient preferences
options.D: Selling herbal supplements to patients to help fund the hospital ward

explanation: Well done! Nurses act as educators and safety advocates, helping patients safely blend alternative methods with their standard medical care.

question: What makes a nursing care plan truly 'individualized' in holistic practice?

options.A: Writing the care plan in medical jargon the patient cannot understand
options.B: Leaving all care planning decisions entirely up to the attending physician
options.C: Using the exact same printed template for every patient with malaria
options.D: Tailoring goals and interventions to the patient's unique lifestyle and values

explanation: That's right! An individualized care plan respects the specific background, preferences, and personal goals of each unique patient.

question: An elderly patient refuses to eat the standard hospital diet because it feels strange to them. What is the best holistic nursing action?

options.A: Report the patient to the medical director for being uncooperative
options.B: Collaborate with the patient to include familiar, culturally accepted local foods
options.C: Force-feed the patient to ensure they meet their daily caloric requirements
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately for refusing hospital dietary guidelines

explanation: Spot on! Holistic care respects cultural preferences and partners with the patient to find workable, comforting dietary solutions.

question: Which of these is NOT a common barrier to holistic nursing practice in busy hospitals?

options.A: Hierarchical medical structures that limit nursing autonomy
options.B: Abundant staffing levels with too many nurses on every shift
options.C: Task-oriented routines focused only on quick medication rounds
options.D: Heavy workloads and high patient-to-nurse ratios

explanation: Great catch! Staff shortages and heavy workloads are major barriers in our hospitals, so abundant staffing is definitely not one of them.

question: How can you deliver holistic care even when working in a busy, understaffed ward?

options.A: By refusing to admit any new patients until the workload lightens
options.B: By delegating all patient contact completely to hospital security guards
options.C: By ignoring all physical medication duties to focus entirely on meditation
options.D: By weaving compassionate communication and a reassuring touch into routine tasks

explanation: Brilliant! Holism doesn't always require extra time. You can easily integrate it into regular nursing duties like bathing a patient or administering medications.

question: What is the main idea behind primary nursing?

options.A: Registered nurses only work during the night shift hours.
options.B: Physicians make all direct bedside nursing assignments for each shift.
options.C: Different nurses perform specific tasks like giving meds or checking vitals.
options.D: One nurse takes 24-hour accountability for a specific patient's care plan.

explanation: You've got this! In primary nursing, one dedicated nurse looks after a patient's complete care plan throughout their stay, even when they're off duty. It builds great nurse-patient trust!

question: How is primary nursing different from traditional task-oriented nursing?

options.A: Task-oriented nursing focuses on splitting chores among staff, whereas primary nursing focuses on holistic, continuous care by one nurse.
options.B: Task-oriented nursing eliminates the need for registered nurses on the hospital floor entirely.
options.C: Primary nursing relies solely on unlicensed assistive personnel for all bedside duties.
options.D: Task-oriented nursing requires patients to change their assigned nurse every single hour.

explanation: Think of task nursing like a factory assembly line where everyone does one chore (like just giving injections), while primary nursing gives one nurse the full picture of the patient's wellbeing.

question: What does decentralized decision-making mean in primary nursing?

options.A: Authority for clinical choices rests directly with the bedside nurse.
options.B: Nurse managers handle every single choice regarding patient hygiene.
options.C: All hospital decisions must be approved by the chief medical director.
options.D: Patients make all of their own medical treatment decisions alone.

explanation: Decentralized just means power is shared! The nurse right there at the bedside has the backing to make immediate, smart clinical choices for their patient.

question: Why is 24-hour accountability so important in primary nursing?

options.A: It ensures consistent, uninterrupted planning and evaluation of patient care across all shifts.
options.B: It forces the primary nurse to stay awake in the hospital for a full day and night.
options.C: It guarantees that physicians do not need to visit the patient after admission.
options.D: It prevents associate nurses from ever touching the patient or charting notes.

explanation: Don't worry, nurses don't stay awake 24 hours! 24-hour accountability means the primary nurse sets the master plan so that even when they go home to rest, other shifts follow that same smooth path.

question: When should discharge planning ideally start in primary nursing?

options.A: When the patient complains about high hospital bills
options.B: Right upon the patient's admission to the unit
options.C: Only after the doctor signs the official discharge papers
options.D: On the exact morning the patient is scheduled to leave

explanation: Smart nursing! We start planning for home the very minute the patient walks through the door so nothing is rushed at the end.

question: A primary nurse notices a prescribed drug dose does not match a patient's failing kidneys. What is the best action?

options.A: Wait until the next shift change to let the incoming nurse deal with it.
options.B: Advocate for the patient by contacting the physician to question the safe dosage.
options.C: Administer the medication anyway since the doctor prescribed it.
options.D: Stop all nursing documentation for the day to avoid liability.

explanation: You are the patient's safety net! Always speak up and check with the doctor if a medication dose looks unsafe for your patient's lab results.

question: What is the main way functional nursing is organized?

options.A: Allowing patients to manage their own treatments without staff help
options.B: Giving one registered nurse total 24-hour responsibility for a single patient
options.C: Assigning specific tasks like medication administration to different staff members
options.D: Having a team leader direct nurse aides to bathe patients

explanation: Functional nursing divides the work by jobs: one person does all dressings, another gives all meds. It's like a production line!

question: Why might a hospital find it hard to use primary nursing instead of team nursing?

options.A: Team nursing requires every single staff member to hold a master's degree.
options.B: Primary nursing completely eliminates the need for any communication with doctors.
options.C: Team nursing prevents nurses from ever talking to patients or families.
options.D: Primary nursing requires a larger proportion of registered nurses, which increases staffing costs.

explanation: Primary nursing needs lots of qualified Registered Nurses to give that individualized care, which can be expensive for hospital management compared to mixing in more junior staff.

question: What is a major benefit of primary nursing for patients?

options.A: Increased feelings of safety and better communication with a consistent nurse
options.B: Shorter waiting times in the hospital cafeteria
options.C: Elimination of all physical pain within twenty-four hours of admission
options.D: Guaranteed zero hospital bills upon discharge

explanation: Patients love seeing a familiar, caring face every day! It builds trust and cuts down the anxiety of hospital stays.

question: What is the biggest threat to keeping a primary nursing unit running smoothly?

options.A: Patients refusing to learn their primary nurse's first name
options.B: Physicians refusing to write orders for patients assigned to primary nurses
options.C: An excess of medical equipment in the hospital storage rooms
options.D: A shortage of qualified registered nurses leading to unmanageable workloads

explanation: When nurse numbers drop too low, it becomes impossible for one nurse to give deep, continuous care to multiple patients at once.

question: Why is true primary nursing often difficult to practice in busy public Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: Severe staff shortages and high nurse-to-patient ratios make 24-hour individual accountability hard to maintain.
options.B: Patients in Nigeria prefer seeing a different nurse every hour for variety.
options.C: Physicians in Nigerian hospitals handle all bedside nursing duties themselves.
options.D: Nigerian nursing councils legally forbid registered nurses from writing patient care plans.

explanation: Real talk: managing a packed ward with limited hands means nurses often have to focus on quick tasks rather than continuous one-on-one primary care.

question: A hospital director in Lagos wants to start primary nursing on a busy surgical ward. What is the best first step?

options.A: Ensure an adequate mix of registered staff and provide training on clinical autonomy.
options.B: Fire all doctors on the ward to give nurses complete control over the hospital.
options.C: Reduce the number of visiting hours to zero minutes per day.
options.D: Ban patients from asking questions about their medications.

explanation: To make primary nursing work, management must first ensure there are enough qualified nurses and empower them to make independent clinical decisions.

question: As a registered nurse working under the team nursing model, what is your primary role on the ward?

options.A: Supervising the doctors during ward rounds
options.B: Performing every single procedure personally for all patients
options.C: Handling only the administrative paperwork for the ward
options.D: Acting as the team leader and taking overall accountability

explanation: Spot on! The registered nurse coordinates the group and takes ultimate responsibility for the care given, even when delegating specific tasks to others. You've got this!

question: Why was the team nursing model originally introduced in healthcare settings?

options.A: To completely eliminate the need for registered nurses
options.B: To cope with nursing shortages and use various staff skills efficiently
options.C: To make patients pay less money for hospital admission
options.D: To reduce the number of doctors needed in the hospital

explanation: Exactly! Team nursing was designed to make the best use of available hands when professional nurses are limited in number. It's all about smart teamwork!

question: Which leadership style works best with the core philosophy of team nursing?

options.A: Democratic leadership involving mutual respect
options.B: Strict autocratic control by auxiliary staff
options.C: Total absence of leadership or direction
options.D: Remote management from outside the hospital

explanation: Well done! Team nursing thrives when the leader respects every member and encourages collaboration instead of just barking harsh commands. Great ward dynamics!

question: How does the team nursing setup benefit junior staff and nursing students on the ward?

options.A: By exempting them from doing any physical patient care
options.B: By allowing them to write hospital policies
options.C: By giving them a supportive environment to learn from senior leaders
options.D: By forcing them to work alone without any supervision

explanation: That's right! Working closely with a registered nurse team leader gives students safe guidance and wonderful practical experience. Every shift is a learning win!

question: In a nursing team, who holds the legal responsibility for assessing patients and planning their care?

options.A: The most junior student nurse
options.B: The team leader who is a registered nurse
options.C: The nursing assistant on duty
options.D: The ward orderly

explanation: Spot on! Assessing patients and planning care requires professional nursing judgment, which is the core duty of the registered nurse team leader.

question: You are working with a nursing assistant on your team. Which of these tasks is safe and appropriate to delegate to them?

options.A: Assisting a stable patient with morning bath and hygiene
options.B: Assessing a newly admitted patient with chest pain
options.C: Administering intravenous medications to a critical patient
options.D: Changing the comprehensive nursing care plan

explanation: Correct! Nursing assistants are wonderful helpers trained for basic comfort measures like hygiene, while medications and assessments need your professional skills.

question: What is the main goal of holding a team nursing conference at the start of a shift?

options.A: To conduct formal examinations for student nurses
options.B: To review patient assignments and plan the shift together
options.C: To discuss hospital financial budgets
options.D: To discipline workers who came late to work

explanation: You got it! The brief conference helps the team connect, share updates, and organize duties so everyone knows what to expect before hitting the floor.

question: Why is clear, open communication during shift handovers so vital in team nursing?

options.A: It makes the shift last longer than necessary
options.B: It ensures that doctors do not speak to nurses
options.C: It prevents fragmented care and catches clinical changes early
options.D: It stops patients from asking questions about their health

explanation: Exactly! Sharing vital updates ensures everyone is on the same page regarding patient status, which keeps our patients safe from errors.

question: What is one of the biggest advantages of using the team nursing model?

options.A: Every single staff member performs the exact same tasks
options.B: Cost-effective use of mixed staff cadres working together
options.C: Complete elimination of any need for supervision
options.D: Patients never have to interact with nursing assistants

explanation: Spot on! Team nursing lets hospitals blend different skill levels efficiently, making patient care well-organized and resourceful.

question: What is a major risk or downside if team leadership on the ward is weak?

options.A: Patients refusing to take any hospital medications
options.B: Automatic promotion of all junior staff members
options.C: Blurred responsibilities and fragmented patient care
options.D: Doctors taking over all nursing responsibilities

explanation: That's right! When leadership lacks clear direction, team members get confused about who is supposed to do what, leading to gaps in patient care.

question: In which care delivery model are duties divided strictly by tasks—like one nurse only giving medications and another only doing wound dressings?

options.A: Primary nursing
options.B: Functional nursing
options.C: Team nursing
options.D: Total patient care

explanation: Correct! Functional nursing focuses on getting specific tasks done across all patients, rather than assigning a whole patient to one nurse.

question: How does team nursing differ from total patient care?

options.A: Total patient care involves no registered nurses at all
options.B: Total patient care is only used in surgical operating theatres
options.C: Team nursing uses a mix of different staff cadres to care for a group of patients
options.D: Team nursing requires one registered nurse to do everything alone

explanation: Well done! Total patient care means one nurse handles everything for a patient, while team nursing shares the workload among a group of mixed staff.

question: What is a major challenge when trying to run team nursing in many Nigerian hospital wards?

options.A: High patient-to-nurse ratios and severe staff shortages
options.B: Complete lack of patients admitted to the wards
options.C: Too many nursing assistants available for every shift
options.D: An excessive number of registered nurses on every ward

explanation: Spot on! Shortages of professional staff make leading teams tough because nurses get overworked and stretched across too many duties.

question: If your ward has a severe shortage of nursing assistants, what is a likely result for you as the registered nurse team leader?

options.A: Being exempted from all clinical ward duties
options.B: Having more time to focus purely on complex patient management
options.C: Spending extra time performing basic domestic or clerical chores
options.D: Automatic promotion to hospital director

explanation: That's correct! When support staff are missing, professional nurses often have to step in to cover basic tasks, which cuts into time for leadership and assessments.

question: What does the health-illness continuum primarily represent?

options.A: A sliding scale of a person's changing health state over time
options.B: A permanent record of a patient's genetic history
options.C: A strict diagnostic checklist for infectious diseases
options.D: A fixed medical category separating the healthy from the sick

explanation: The continuum demonstrates that health changes constantly rather than staying in a fixed state. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why can a patient with a chronic illness still be placed toward the high-wellness end of the continuum?

options.A: Chronic illnesses automatically cure themselves over time
options.B: Medical tests cannot detect chronic conditions on the continuum
options.C: A chronic diagnosis means the disease has completely gone away
options.D: They can achieve a good quality of life and manage their symptoms well

explanation: Wellness involves mental and social well-being alongside physical status, allowing people with chronic conditions to feel well. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which term describes an objective and measurable alteration in body function?

options.A: Disease
options.B: Wellness
options.C: Illness
options.D: Continuum

explanation: Disease refers to the pathological changes inside the body that medical tests can measure and detect. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main difference between illness and disease?

options.A: Illness is how the person feels and experiences their sickness, while disease is the medical pathology
options.B: Illness can only be diagnosed with lab tests, while disease is purely psychological
options.C: Disease is a subjective feeling, whereas illness is an objective medical label
options.D: There is no practical difference between the two terms in nursing

explanation: Illness is subjective and personal, while disease is the clinical pathology diagnosed by a doctor. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h2)

question: What are social determinants of health?

options.A: Conditions in the environments where people are born, live, and work
options.B: Internal genetic mutations inherited directly from parents
options.C: The specific lab values recorded during a hospital admission
options.D: A patient's personal attitude toward taking prescribed medications

explanation: Social determinants include housing, income, education, and community environment which heavily influence health. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h3)

question: A patient with frequent malaria infections lives in a neighborhood with stagnant drainage water and poor housing. Which factor is most directly influencing this patient's health?

options.A: A lack of personal interest in health education
options.B: An unavoidable genetic predisposition to mosquito bites
options.C: Environmental and social determinants of health
options.D: An acute psychological response to stress

explanation: Poor living conditions and stagnant water are environmental factors that directly increase exposure to illness. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h3)

question: Giving routine childhood immunizations falls under which level of prevention?

options.A: Quaternary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Secondary prevention

explanation: Primary prevention stops diseases from occurring in the first place through measures like vaccination and health promotion. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is routine screening for high blood pressure classified as secondary prevention?

options.A: It completely prevents a person from ever developing hypertension
options.B: It is only performed after a patient has suffered a major stroke
options.C: It catches an existing condition early before severe complications develop
options.D: It focuses purely on physical rehabilitation in a hospital ward

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis and screening so treatment can start early. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary focus of nursing when promoting wellness along the continuum?

options.A: Empowering patients through education, support, and holistic assessment
options.B: Directing patients to ignore lifestyle factors and rely only on drugs
options.C: Controlling all aspects of a patient's personal daily routine
options.D: Solely diagnosing medical diseases and prescribing surgical treatments

explanation: Nurses focus on helping patients understand their bodies and adopt healthy habits to move toward wellness. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which action best demonstrates a nurse acting to promote wellness?

options.A: Teaching a community group about balanced diets and regular exercise
options.B: Discharging a patient without giving any instructions on home care
options.C: Refusing to answer questions about a patient's prescribed diet
options.D: Waiting until a chronic disease becomes terminal before intervening

explanation: Health education and lifestyle promotion are core nursing interventions for wellness. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h5)

question: A community health nurse in a rural Nigerian village organizes an outreach to teach mothers how to mix oral rehydration salts for diarrhea. What type of intervention is this?

options.A: A purely administrative task unrelated to patient welfare
options.B: A tertiary action meant exclusively for chronic surgical patients
options.C: An unnecessary hospital procedure reserved only for intensive care units
options.D: A practical community-level nursing intervention promoting health recovery

explanation: Community outreach brings essential health knowledge directly to where people live to prevent severe illness. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why must nurses in local community clinics look beyond hospital walls when caring for patients?

options.A: Environmental and economic living conditions heavily impact health outcomes
options.B: Nurses are forbidden from providing care outside of enclosed rooms
options.C: Community members never visit hospitals for severe medical problems
options.D: Lab tests can only be accurately performed in outdoor market stalls

explanation: Understanding a patient's home and community environment helps explain why illnesses occur and how to prevent them. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary definition of homeostasis in the human body?

options.A: Stopping all electrical activity in the brain
options.B: Rapidly fluctuating blood pressure levels
options.C: Constantly increasing metabolic activity
options.D: Maintaining a stable internal environment

explanation: Homeostasis refers to the body's continuous effort to keep its internal conditions stable and balanced despite external changes. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which body system primarily controls automatic physiological adaptations like heart rate and sweating?

options.A: The skeletal muscle system
options.B: The voluntary somatic system
options.C: The autonomic nervous system
options.D: The lymphatic filtration system

explanation: The autonomic nervous system manages involuntary body functions and automatic stress responses without requiring conscious thought. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the correct chronological order of the three stages in the General Adaptation Syndrome?

options.A: Alarm, exhaustion, resistance
options.B: Resistance, alarm, exhaustion
options.C: Exhaustion, resistance, alarm
options.D: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion

explanation: The body first experiences a sudden alarm, tries to resist the ongoing stress, and finally reaches exhaustion if the stress is too prolonged. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h2)

question: A patient has been dealing with severe chronic financial and physical stress for over a year and now has a failing immune system and frequent infections. Which stage of GAS are they experiencing?

options.A: Stage of resistance
options.B: Homeostatic baseline stage
options.C: Stage of exhaustion
options.D: Alarm reaction stage

explanation: Prolonged stress depletes the body's energy reserves, leading to organ failure and immune collapse during the exhaustion stage. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the main difference between problem-focused and emotion-focused coping?

options.A: Emotion-focused fixes physical organs, while problem-focused cures mental illness
options.B: Problem-focused is always unhealthy, while emotion-focused is always beneficial
options.C: Problem-focused involves denial, while emotion-focused involves physical exercise
options.D: Problem-focused deals with the actual stressor, while emotion-focused manages feelings about it

explanation: Problem-focused coping targets the root cause of stress, whereas emotion-focused coping helps soothe the emotional distress caused by the situation. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why might a newly diagnosed patient temporarily use the defense mechanism of denial?

options.A: To protect the mind from overwhelming emotional pain
options.B: To increase their physical strength and immunity
options.C: To speed up cellular regeneration and wound healing
options.D: To permanently cure their underlying medical condition

explanation: Defense mechanisms like denial act as psychological buffers, shielding the individual from sudden, unbearable emotional shocks. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized factor that influences a patient's ability to adapt to an illness?

options.A: Past life experiences and trauma
options.B: The hospital's interior wall color
options.C: Cultural beliefs regarding health
options.D: Available social and family support

explanation: Internal and external factors like culture, support systems, and personal history deeply affect adaptation, whereas minor environmental aesthetics do not dictate coping capacity. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h4)

question: How does low socioeconomic status typically impact a patient's long-term adaptation to a chronic illness?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for professional nursing care
options.B: It forces the body to stop experiencing the alarm stage of stress
options.C: It automatically guarantees a faster psychological recovery
options.D: It can limit access to essential medications and healthy nutrition

explanation: Financial hardship restricts access to necessary health resources, making sustained disease management and adaptation significantly harder. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is a common clinical pitfall when dealing with a patient showing signs of maladaptation?

options.A: Encouraging them to express their hidden fears and worries
options.B: Providing too much detailed education about their medication
options.C: Labeling the patient as difficult instead of recognizing psychological exhaustion
options.D: Checking their vital signs too frequently throughout the day

explanation: Viewing uncooperative behavior as a character flaw rather than a coping failure prevents nurses from offering the proper psychological support. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h5)

question: A hospitalized patient refuses to eat, avoids talking to staff, and expresses hopelessness about recovery. Which nursing conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: The patient is using problem-focused coping to solve their illness
options.B: The patient has fully adapted to the hospital environment
options.C: The patient has successfully achieved the stage of resistance in GAS
options.D: The patient is displaying signs of maladaptation and needs psychological support

explanation: Withdrawal and hopelessness indicate poor adjustment to illness, pointing directly toward maladaptation requiring intervention. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h5)

question: A newly admitted patient is shaking and terrified of an upcoming surgical procedure. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Delay informing the doctor until the surgery is about to start
options.B: Use a calm voice, establish trust, and explain procedures simply
options.C: Tell the patient that fear is irrational and demand they calm down
options.D: Leave the patient alone in the room until they stop shaking

explanation: Establishing a trusting, calm environment helps reduce acute anxiety and supports the patient's psychological adaptation to stress. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why is it helpful to involve patients in small self-care tasks during recovery?

options.A: It forces the body to skip the alarm stage of the GAS model
options.B: It guarantees that no complications will ever develop
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any medications
options.D: It restores a sense of personal control and reduces helplessness

explanation: Active participation empowers patients, countering the loss of control often brought on by severe illness and hospitalization. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T6#GNS123_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the main goal of homeostasis in the human body?

options.A: Increasing body temperature continuously
options.B: Keeping a stable internal environment
options.C: Stopping all metabolic activities
options.D: Speeding up the aging process

explanation: You've got this! Homeostasis simply means keeping your body's internal environment nice and steady, even when things change around you. Think of it as your body's built-in thermostat.

question: Why is keeping a narrow range for vital signs important for a patient?

options.A: It ensures the patient stays awake during the night
options.B: It guarantees that blood pressure never changes
options.C: It prevents vital organs from failing due to extreme stress
options.D: It stops the patient from needing any medication

explanation: Great thinking! Staying within a safe, normal range protects your patient's cells and organs from being overworked by extreme highs and lows.

question: Which part of a feedback loop is responsible for detecting a change in the body?

options.A: Set point
options.B: Receptor
options.C: Effector
options.D: Control center

explanation: Spot on! Receptors act as your body's scouts or sensors, picking up any changes (stimuli) in your internal or external environment.

question: How does negative feedback differ from positive feedback?

options.A: Negative feedback speeds up heart rate, while positive feedback slows it down
options.B: Negative feedback only works in the brain, while positive feedback works in the skin
options.C: Negative feedback causes disease, while positive feedback cures it
options.D: Negative feedback reverses a change, while positive feedback amplifies it

explanation: Don't let the names fool you! Negative feedback works to bring levels back down to normal (like cooling down when you're hot), while positive feedback pushes a change further until a task is done (like during childbirth).

question: What is the normal pH range for human blood?
explanation: Spot on! Blood pH is tightly kept between 7.35 and 7.45 so that enzymes and vital body processes can run smoothly.

question: A patient is admitted with severe vomiting and diarrhea. Which imbalance are they most at risk for developing?

options.A: Fluid and electrolyte imbalance
options.B: Excessive weight gain
options.C: Permanent high blood pressure
options.D: Chronic respiratory alkalosis

explanation: Exactly! Vomiting and diarrhea flush out body fluids and essential minerals super fast, leaving the patient low on water and electrolytes.

question: What triggers a homeostatic imbalance in the human body?

options.A: When a person sleeps for more than eight hours
options.B: When disease or trauma overwhelms normal control systems
options.C: When vital signs stay completely stable for a long time
options.D: When the body eats a balanced diet with fresh fruits

explanation: Well done! When illness or injury hits hard, it can strain or break the natural feedback loops that keep the body balanced.

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical result of a major homeostatic breakdown?

options.A: Uncontrolled blood sugar spikes
options.B: Dangerous shifts in blood pH
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Balanced electrolyte levels in the blood

explanation: You got it! Balanced electrolytes mean homeostasis is winning and doing its job, not that it has broken down.

question: Why are vital sign trends over several hours more useful than a single reading?

options.A: They prevent the need to perform laboratory blood tests
options.B: They take less time for the nurse to chart
options.C: They show whether the patient is improving or getting worse over time
options.D: They guarantee that the electronic monitor is working correctly

explanation: Brilliant nursing insight! Tracking patterns helps you catch subtle warning signs before a patient takes a turn for the worse.

question: Which physical sign is a reliable indicator that vital organs are getting enough blood flow?

options.A: Dry and cracked lips
options.B: Adequate urine output
options.C: Slow and deep breathing
options.D: Cold and pale fingers

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Good urine output tells you the kidneys are well-perfused, meaning the heart and blood vessels are keeping good pressure up.

question: A patient presents with low blood pressure and dry mucous membranes due to fluid loss. Which nursing intervention best supports fluid homeostasis?

options.A: Administering a medication to raise heart rate
options.B: Encouraging strict bed rest without fluids
options.C: Applying a cooling blanket to lower fever
options.D: Administering prescribed intravenous fluids

explanation: Correct! Giving IV fluids directly replaces the lost volume, bringing blood pressure and circulation back to a safe zone.

question: How do nursing interventions help restore balance in a sick patient?

options.A: By stopping the patient from eating or drinking
options.B: By supporting or taking over failing regulatory systems
options.C: By replacing all natural body organs with machines
options.D: By curing viral infections without the use of drugs

explanation: Exactly right! As a nurse, you step in to help with breathing, hydration, or circulation whenever the patient's body needs backup.

question: What happens when homeostatic failure is left untreated for too long?

options.A: Vital organs begin to shut down and shock can occur
options.B: The patient enters a state of deep relaxation
options.C: The body automatically fixes itself without any help
options.D: Blood pressure rises to a very safe level

explanation: Spot on. If the body's regulatory systems stay broken down, tissues are starved of oxygen, which can quickly lead to organ failure and shock.

question: What is the term for a dangerous loop where low blood pressure weakens the heart, which then lowers blood pressure even further?

options.A: An adaptive resting phase
options.B: A normal healthy recovery process
options.C: A stable metabolic equilibrium
options.D: A positive feedback spiral toward shock

explanation: You've got it! This is a classic runaway positive feedback loop where each problem makes the next one worse, pulling the patient deeper into danger if we don't intervene.

question: What is the correct order of the three stages in Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome?

options.A: Alarm, exhaustion, resistance
options.B: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
options.C: Exhaustion, resistance, alarm
options.D: Resistance, alarm, exhaustion

explanation: Think of it as a journey: your body first sounds the alarm when stressed, tries to fight back during resistance, and finally gets worn out in exhaustion if the stress doesn't stop. You've got this!

question: What happens in the body during the resistance stage of stress?

options.A: The sympathetic nervous system shuts down completely
options.B: Energy reserves are fully depleted and the person collapses
options.C: The body attempts to adapt and cope with the ongoing stressor
options.D: No hormonal or physiological changes take place

explanation: During resistance, your body tries its best to balance things out and keep functioning despite the ongoing pressure. It's like your internal battery working overtime to keep you going!

question: Which gland releases cortisol when signaled by the pituitary gland during stress?

options.A: Adrenal cortex
options.B: Thyroid gland
options.C: Pineal gland
options.D: Pancreas

explanation: The outer layer of your adrenal glands (right above your kidneys) is called the adrenal cortex, and it pumps out cortisol to help you handle stress.

question: What is the main job of cortisol during the stress response?

options.A: To lower blood pressure and slow down breathing
options.B: To enhance immune system activity and fight infection
options.C: To raise blood glucose and supply energy to vital organs
options.D: To stimulate digestion and nutrient absorption

explanation: Cortisol acts like an emergency power switch, boosting your blood sugar so your brain and muscles have the immediate fuel they need to react.

question: Which of these is a classic example of a physical stressor?

options.A: A difficult exam
options.B: Severe burn injury
options.C: Financial debt
options.D: Workplace bullying

explanation: A burn directly harms the physical tissues of the body, making it a physical stressor. The others are mental or social stressors!

question: How do chronic stressors differ from acute stressors?

options.A: Chronic stressors only affect psychological well-being
options.B: Acute stressors last for months or years
options.C: Chronic stressors persist over a long period without relief
options.D: Acute stressors cause no physiological response

explanation: Think of acute stress as a sudden flash flood (short and intense), while chronic stress is like a long-term drought that wears you down over months or years.

question: Which symptom is a common physical sign of high stress?

options.A: Complete paralysis of the limbs
options.B: Uncontrollable tremors in the legs
options.C: Muscle tension and headaches
options.D: Joint swelling and redness

explanation: When stressed, we often clench our muscles without realizing it, which frequently leads to tight shoulders, sore muscles, and tension headaches.

question: A patient visits the clinic with stomach upset, tension headaches, and poor sleep after getting a major promotion at work. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Symptoms of an acute bacterial gastrointestinal infection
options.B: Early warning signs of a neurodegenerative disorder
options.C: Adverse reaction to routine vaccination
options.D: Physiological and psychological manifestations of acute stress

explanation: Even good life changes can overwhelm the body! These physical aches and sleep troubles are classic signs that stress is taking a toll.

question: What is a key physical sign that a patient is feeling very stressed?

options.A: Relaxed facial muscles
options.B: Calm and steady posture
options.C: Deep, slow breathing
options.D: Pacing and restlessness

explanation: When the 'fight-or-flight' response kicks in, people often find it hard to sit still, resulting in fidgeting, pacing, or jittery movements.

question: Why do nurses use tools like the Perceived Stress Scale during patient assessments?

options.A: To replace physical examinations and vital signs
options.B: To measure the patient's exact blood cortisol levels
options.C: To diagnose specific psychiatric disorders definitively
options.D: To quantify the patient's subjective feelings of stress

explanation: Everyone feels stress differently. These scales help nurses turn a patient's personal feeling of overwhelm into clear information so they can give the best care.

question: What term describes the wear and tear on the body from long-term, ongoing stress?

options.A: Systemic exhaustion
options.B: Adverse adaptation
options.C: Allostatic load
options.D: Homeostatic balance

explanation: 'Allostatic load' is just a fancy way of saying your body gets tired and worn down from fighting stress day after day without a break.

question: How can chronic stress lead to heart disease over time?

options.A: By slowing down the heart rate to dangerous levels
options.B: By causing sudden enlargement of heart valves
options.C: By maintaining high blood pressure and damaging arterial walls
options.D: By reducing the amount of blood pumped by the heart

explanation: When stress hormones keep your blood pressure high day after day, it slowly damages your blood vessels, making it easier for plaque to build up.

question: Which nervous system kicks in when a patient practices slow, deep breathing?

options.A: Central nervous system
options.B: Somatic nervous system
options.C: Parasympathetic nervous system
options.D: Sympathetic nervous system

explanation: Deep breathing signals your vagus nerve to turn on the parasympathetic system—your body's wonderful 'rest-and-digest' mode that cools everything down.

question: A patient is anxious and has a rapid heart rate before surgery. Which nursing action is best to help calm them?

options.A: Advise the patient to ignore the upcoming surgery entirely
options.B: Leave the patient alone in a brightly lit room to rest
options.C: Guide the patient through slow deep breathing exercises
options.D: Encourage the patient to drink several cups of strong coffee

explanation: Taking slow, deep breaths is a simple, powerful way to quiet the fight-or-flight response, slow down a racing heart, and ease pre-surgery nerves.

question: What do we mean by "illness behaviour"?

options.A: The laboratory test results confirming an infection
options.B: The permanent physical damage caused by a disease
options.C: How a doctor chooses the correct medication dosage
options.D: How a person responds to symptoms and seeks help

explanation: Think of illness behaviour as the steps people take when something feels off in their body—ranging from staying home to rest, to visiting the clinic for help. You've got this!

question: Why might two different people with the same medical condition react completely differently?

options.A: Doctors always prescribe different treatments for identical diseases
options.B: Disease is purely subjective while illness is objective
options.C: Illness is the personal experience and interpretation of symptoms
options.D: Physical pathology dictates every single action a person takes

explanation: Disease is what the body has, but illness is how the person feels and experiences it. Everyone's perspective is unique!

question: What is the very first thing that happens when someone starts to fall ill?

options.A: The patient hands over control to the doctor
options.B: The nurse performs a full physical assessment
options.C: The individual completely returns to work
options.D: The person notices a physical change or symptom

explanation: It always starts with perception! You first notice that something feels unusual in your body before taking any other step.

question: A patient agrees they are sick, stays home from classes, and asks family members if they look feverish. Which stage of illness is this?

options.A: Assumption of the sick role
options.B: Recovery and rehabilitation
options.C: Symptom experience
options.D: Dependent-patient role

explanation: When you step back from your daily duties and look for validation from loved ones that you need rest, you've entered the sick role.

question: Transport fare and hospital registration costs can heavily influence whether a person visits the clinic. What kind of factor is this?

options.A: Pain tolerance level
options.B: Financial status
options.C: Biological immunity
options.D: Genetic predisposition

explanation: Money matters! Financial resources play a massive role in whether patients can afford to seek care or buy their drugs on time.

question: How can a terrible past experience at a hospital affect a patient's future health choices?

options.A: It eliminates all anxiety related to surgical procedures
options.B: It guarantees the person will follow all doctor's orders
options.C: It automatically cures their current physical condition
options.D: It may make the person avoid or delay seeking medical care

explanation: Bad experiences build fear and distrust. As future nurses, we always want to make our clinics welcoming so patients don't run away from care!

question: How does culture influence a person's health-seeking habits?

options.A: It dictates the exact laboratory values for blood pressure
options.B: It determines the anatomical structure of human organs
options.C: It prevents individuals from ever feeling physical pain
options.D: It shapes how they view, express, and seek treatment for sickness

explanation: Culture guides our beliefs! It teaches us how to talk about pain, who to consult first, and what healing should look like.

question: Why is it important for nurses to ask patients about traditional or local remedies they might be using?

options.A: Cultural beliefs have zero impact on modern hospital treatment
options.B: Patients may combine traditional remedies with prescribed hospital drugs
options.C: Nurses must enforce orthodox medicine by confiscating herbs
options.D: Traditional practices completely replace the need for physical exams

explanation: Many patients mix hospital meds with local herbs. Knowing this helps us watch out for dangerous drug clashes while respecting their beliefs.

question: What do we mean by "abnormal illness behaviour"?

options.A: Seeking help immediately after experiencing severe trauma
options.B: A response that is out of proportion to actual physical findings
options.C: Following all medical advice given by the attending nurse
options.D: Recovering from a minor illness within expected timeframes

explanation: This happens when the reaction doesn't match the medical reality—like complete denial of a serious condition, or intense panic over a tiny scratch.

question: A patient with stable blood pressure keeps coming back, demanding brain scans because they are convinced they have a fatal tumour, despite clear test results. What is this called?

options.A: Health anxiety
options.B: Symptom denial
options.C: Stoic endurance
options.D: Normal recovery

explanation: When someone constantly worries they have a severe illness despite all medical proof to the contrary, it points toward health anxiety.

question: Which question is best when a nurse wants to understand how a patient is coping with their sickness?

options.A: Can you tell me your home address and phone number?
options.B: Did you take your prescribed blood pressure pill?
options.C: What is your exact weight in kilograms today?
options.D: How has this sickness affected your daily life?

explanation: Open-ended questions like this give patients room to express their feelings, struggles, and how the illness is impacting them personally.

question: Why must nurses look beyond vital signs when assessing a patient?

options.A: Doctors handle physical assessments while nurses only do paperwork
options.B: Physical numbers do not show how the patient emotionally experiences the disease
options.C: Vital signs are completely useless in clinical nursing practice
options.D: Patients never tell the truth about their physical pain levels

explanation: Vital signs tell us about the body, but talking to the patient tells us about their fears, coping skills, and emotional state.

question: What is the best way to handle a patient who is extremely anxious about minor symptoms?

options.A: Scold them for wasting valuable hospital time
options.B: Discharge them immediately from the clinic ward
options.C: Validate their feelings and offer gentle reassurance
options.D: Ignore their complaints until lab results come out

explanation: Never dismiss their fear! Validating their emotions builds instant trust and helps them calm down.

question: Which of these actions should a nurse NOT take when dealing with unhelpful illness behaviour?

options.A: Listen actively to the patient's underlying fears
options.B: Argue aggressively to prove the patient is completely wrong
options.C: Involve medical social workers for holistic support
options.D: Provide clear and simple education about warning signs

explanation: Arguing never works in nursing! It breaks trust and spikes anxiety. We guide with empathy and gentle education instead.

question: A patient tells you they have a terrible headache. What kind of data is this?

options.A: Subjective data
options.B: Diagnostic data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Objective data

explanation: You got this! Subjective data is what the patient tells you (their symptoms and feelings). Since you can't measure a headache with a machine, it's subjective. Think 'S' for Subjective and 'S' for Spoken by the patient!

question: Why do we take a baseline assessment when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: It helps the nurse detect small changes in the patient's condition over time.
options.B: It replaces the need to review previous medical history charts.
options.C: It eliminates the need to perform further physical examinations during the shift.
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will experience a rapid recovery.

explanation: Spot on! A baseline is your starting point. Knowing where your patient starts helps you easily spot if they are getting better or worse during your shift.

question: In the PQRST pain assessment tool, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?

options.A: Quietness
options.B: Quickness
options.C: Quality
options.D: Quantity

explanation: Great job! 'Q' stands for Quality. It means asking the patient to describe what the pain feels like—is it sharp, dull, stabbing, or throbbing?

question: A patient tells you that both of their parents have high blood pressure and diabetes. Where should you write this?

options.A: Past medical history
options.B: History of present illness
options.C: Review of systems
options.D: Family history

explanation: Spot on! Information about blood relatives (like parents and siblings) always goes into the family history section so you can check for genetic risks.

question: When examining the tummy, why do we listen (auscultate) before we press (palpate)?

options.A: Auscultation requires deep pressure that must be done first.
options.B: Patients find palpation relaxing after listening to bowel sounds.
options.C: Palpation can alter or stimulate bowel sounds, making them inaccurate.
options.D: Standard hospital policy dictates this order for all body systems.

explanation: You're doing great! If you press or massage the tummy first, you wake up the bowels and make them make extra noise. Always listen first to catch their natural sounds!

question: Which physical exam technique involves tapping on the body to check what is underneath?

options.A: Palpation
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Inspection
options.D: Auscultation

explanation: Spot on! Percussion is like playing a small drum on the skin. The sound tells you if the organ underneath is full of air, fluid, or solid.

question: What is the most reliable way to know how much pain a patient is feeling?

options.A: Changes in the patient's heart rate
options.B: The patient's own self-report
options.C: Family members' interpretation
options.D: The nurse's clinical observation

explanation: Exactly! Pain is whatever the patient says it is. Their personal word is always the gold standard for pain assessment.

question: Which of these is an example of non-pharmacological (drug-free) pain relief?

options.A: Applying a warm compress to a sore muscle
options.B: Administering a prescribed dose of oral ibuprofen
options.C: Dispensing a scheduled narcotic pain pill
options.D: Injecting intravenous morphine into the patient port

explanation: You got it! Warm compresses, massage, and changing positions help ease pain without using drugs (pharmaceuticals).

question: Why do nurses do a cultural assessment for patients?

options.A: To satisfy mandatory hospital paperwork requirements only
options.B: To convince the patient to adopt Western medical practices
options.C: To understand the patient's beliefs and values in order to provide individualized care
options.D: To determine the financial income of the patient's household

explanation: Wonderful! Cultural assessments help us respect our patients' traditions and beliefs, making sure our care fits their unique lifestyle.

question: Which of the following is part of a psychosocial assessment?

options.A: Checking the range of motion in the patient's knee joint
options.B: Evaluating the patient's coping mechanisms and support systems
options.C: Listening for abnormal breath sounds in the lower lobes
options.D: Reviewing lab results for elevated white blood cells

explanation: Spot on! Psychosocial checks look at mental health, how well the patient handles stress, and who is there to support them at home.

question: Why should a nurse look at laboratory results together with the physical exam instead of looking at labs alone?

options.A: Laboratory values are often incorrect and need physical confirmation.
options.B: Physical assessments can change laboratory values within minutes.
options.C: Hospital regulations forbid doctors from looking at labs without a nurse present.
options.D: Labs only provide part of the clinical picture and require patient context to be meaningful.

explanation: You nailed it! Numbers on a lab report don't tell the whole story. You always pair them with how the patient actually looks and feels.

question: An elevated white blood cell (WBC) count usually points to what in a patient?

options.A: Severe dehydration
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Chronic kidney failure
options.D: Infection or inflammation

explanation: Great job! White blood cells are our body's soldiers. When they shoot up in number, it usually means they are busy fighting off an infection or inflammation.

question: What does the letter 'S' stand for at the very beginning of the SBAR communication tool?

options.A: Solution
options.B: Situation
options.C: Severity
options.D: Symptoms

explanation: Spot on! In SBAR, the first 'S' is for Situation—a quick summary of what is happening right now that made you call or report.

question: Which of these is an example of clean, objective nursing documentation?

options.A: Patient was acting cranky and complaining about unnecessary hospital food today.
options.B: Patient is likely faking discomfort to get more pain medication from the nurse.
options.C: Patient stated, 'My stomach hurts,' and grimaced when palpated in the right lower quadrant.
options.D: Patient seemed to be in terrible pain and refused to cooperate with staff.

explanation: You're a star! Objective notes stick to exact patient quotes and things you can actually see or feel, without adding personal judgments like 'cranky' or 'faking'.

question: When you look at a standard X-ray, what color do dense structures like bones usually appear?

options.A: Bright green
options.B: Pitch black
options.C: Bright white
options.D: Transparent clear

explanation: Bones block the X-ray beams from passing through to the film, creating a bright white picture. You've got this!

question: Why is it super helpful for nurses to understand basic X-ray imaging?

options.A: To replace the radiologist in reading films
options.B: To prescribe the correct radiation dosage
options.C: To operate the heavy X-ray machine safely
options.D: To help coordinate care and ease patient anxiety

explanation: As a nurse, you are the friendly face who prepares patients and calms their nerves before procedures. Great nursing starts with great communication!

question: What are the three golden rules of radiation safety?

options.A: Light, heat, and pressure
options.B: Height, weight, and volume
options.C: Time, distance, and shielding
options.D: Speed, velocity, and mass

explanation: Always remember: spend less time near radiation, step back to create distance, and use lead shielding. Safety first!

question: How does stepping further away from an active X-ray source affect your radiation exposure?

options.A: Exposure stays exactly the same
options.B: Exposure increases rapidly
options.C: Exposure turns into heat energy
options.D: Exposure decreases significantly

explanation: Radiation spreads out as it travels. The further away you stand, the safer you are!

question: What is a standard chest X-ray most commonly used to check for in the ward?

options.A: Viewing active blood flow inside brain tissue
options.B: Checking for pneumonia or heart enlargement
options.C: Measuring exact electrical heart rhythms
options.D: Detecting microscopic bacterial infections in blood

explanation: Chest X-rays give us a clear view of the lungs and heart size, making them perfect for spotting conditions like pneumonia.

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with severe lower right chest pain after a motorcycle fall. Which test is the doctor likely to order first?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Electrocardiogram
options.C: Urinalysis
options.D: Lumbar puncture

explanation: After chest trauma, an X-ray is the quickest way to check for broken ribs or bruised lungs. You're building great clinical instincts!

question: Why do we ask patients to take off all jewelry and metallic objects before an X-ray?

options.A: They make the patient feel too heavy on the table
options.B: They attract stray electrical currents from the machine
options.C: They cause the X-ray tube to overheat quickly
options.D: They create dense white artifacts that hide details

explanation: Metal blocks X-rays completely, leaving bright white spots that might hide important clues on the film.

question: What is a vital safety question a nurse must ask a young female patient before a pelvic or abdominal X-ray?

options.A: Do you have a history of high blood pressure?
options.B: Have you ever had a blood transfusion?
options.C: Could you possibly be pregnant?
options.D: What is your normal daily diet?

explanation: Radiation can harm a growing baby, so checking for pregnancy beforehand is a crucial safety step for every female of childbearing age.

question: Why are patients usually asked to hold their breath for a quick second during a chest X-ray?

options.A: To prevent radiation from entering the stomach
options.B: To prevent motion blur and clearly view lung fields
options.C: To lower their blood pressure during the flash
options.D: To make the heart beat slower for the picture

explanation: Breathing makes the chest move, which blurs the picture. Holding still gives us a crystal-clear image!

question: Which of these is NOT a normal nursing duty when taking a patient for an X-ray?

options.A: Monitoring oxygen therapy levels during transport
options.B: Developing the X-ray films in the darkroom
options.C: Explaining positioning steps to calm the patient
options.D: Ensuring intravenous lines have adequate slack

explanation: Developing films is the job of the radiographer, while keeping the patient safe and comfortable is your superpower as a nurse!

question: How do hospitals keep imaging going during sudden power outages?

options.A: Utilizing backup generators and battery-powered portable units
options.B: Performing manual sketches of internal organs at the bedside
options.C: Canceling all diagnostic imaging tests for the entire week
options.D: Waiting indefinitely until the public electricity grid restores power

explanation: Backup generators and portable machines are lifesavers when the main power grid goes down in clinical settings.

question: You are in a busy radiology department with a stable routine patient and an emergency trauma patient who is struggling to breathe. Who gets imaged first?

options.A: Prioritize the unstable trauma patient for immediate imaging
options.B: Send both patients in together to save time
options.C: Tell the trauma patient to wait in the normal queue
options.D: Cancel both appointments and reschedule for next month

explanation: Emergency and unstable patients always come first so we can catch and treat life-threatening issues right away.

question: What type of energy does an ultrasound machine use to create images inside the body?

options.A: Sound waves
options.B: Magnetic fields
options.C: Radioactive tracers
options.D: X-ray radiation

explanation: Ultrasound uses safe, high-frequency sound waves that bounce off your tissues to form a picture, meaning there's no radiation involved at all!

question: Why do doctors and nurses prefer ultrasound when a patient needs repeated scans over a short time?

options.A: it does not use harmful ionizing radiation
options.B: It is totally painless and needs no practice
options.C: It gives a much clearer view of bones than a CT scan
options.D: It completely replaces the need for blood tests

explanation: Because it lacks harmful radiation, ultrasound is super safe and can be repeated as many times as needed to monitor healing.

question: Why do we apply that slippery water-based gel to a patient's skin before doing an ultrasound?

options.A: To get rid of air pockets that block sound waves
options.B: To cool down the hot scanner probe
options.C: To numb the skin so the scan doesn't hurt
options.D: To leave a mark on the skin for later

explanation: Sound waves struggle to travel through air. The gel acts like a bridge, helping the waves glide smoothly into the body.

question: How do hard structures like bones usually look on a standard ultrasound image?

options.A: As glowing green areas showing high activity
options.B: They block the sound and leave a dark shadow behind them
options.C: As completely clear, empty spaces
options.D: As bright white lines that let sound pass right through

explanation: Bone bounces most of the sound back, preventing the waves from going deeper—this creates what we call an acoustic shadow behind it.

question: Which type of ultrasound is best when you need to check how fast and in what direction blood is flowing?

options.A: Doppler ultrasound
options.B: Static X-ray mode
options.C: M-Mode ultrasound
options.D: B-Mode ultrasound

explanation: Doppler is your go-to scan for blood vessels because it specifically tracks moving red blood cells to measure flow.

question: What does a regular B-Mode ultrasound show you on the screen?

options.A: A bright color map of bone strength
options.B: A two-dimensional greyscale picture of internal organs
options.C: A live wave graph of the heart's electrical rhythm
options.D: A 3D heat map of the body's temperature

explanation: Think of B-Mode as your standard black-and-white anatomical view that outlines the shape and structure of organs.

question: Which of these common health issues is an abdominal ultrasound usually ordered to check?

options.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.B: Gallstones hiding in the gallbladder
options.C: A broken bone in the lower leg
options.D: Bacterial meningitis in the spine

explanation: Ultrasound is brilliant at looking inside fluid-filled organs like the gallbladder to spot stones or blockages.

question: A patient comes in with a suspected blood clot in their leg vein (deep vein thrombosis). What scan will the doctor likely order?

options.A: Renal B-Mode ultrasound
options.B: Pelvic M-Mode ultrasound
options.C: Cardiac echocardiogram
options.D: Vascular Doppler ultrasound

explanation: A vascular Doppler scan is specifically designed to peek inside blood vessels and catch clots early.

question: Why is a patient scheduled for an abdominal ultrasound usually told to fast (no food or water) for a few hours beforehand?

options.A: To keep their blood pressure steady before the scan
options.B: To cut down on tummy gas and keep the gallbladder full
options.C: To make sure they have an empty bladder for a pelvic check
options.D: To stop them from throwing up during the procedure

explanation: Food creates gas that blocks sound waves, and fasting keeps the gallbladder nice and full so it's easy to see!

question: Why are patients told to drink water and hold their urine before a pelvic ultrasound?

options.A: A full bladder pushes pelvic organs up into a better viewing position
options.B: To encourage bowel movements before the scan
options.C: A full bladder is needed to turn on the color Doppler
options.D: To stop them from getting dehydrated during the test

explanation: A distended bladder acts like a clear window, pushing gas-out of the way and giving a fantastic view of pelvic structures.

question: As a nurse assisting with an ultrasound-guided needle procedure, what is your most important duty?

options.A: Adjusting the machine's sound frequency during the scan
options.B: Keeping the area strictly sterile and helping the patient stay still
options.C: Giving the patient general anesthesia
options.D: Reading and writing the final report

explanation: Invasive bedside procedures need strict infection control and a steady patient to keep everything safe and accurate.

question: Why might a nurse position an abdominal ultrasound patient to lie on their left side?

options.A: To stop them from rolling off the bed
options.B: To shift bowel gas away from the organs being checked
options.C: To boost their blood pressure for the Doppler scan
options.D: To relax their tummy muscles completely

explanation: Shifting the patient's position helps move pesky gas-filled loops of the bowel out of the way of the ultrasound beam.

question: What is an immediate nursing task to take care of right after an ultrasound scan ends?
